comparator.name: Bachelor European Law School
comparator.sourceNotes: The adopted 2026–2027 regulations specify 60 EC of compulsory study in each of the first two years, followed by a 48 EC restricted elective phase and the 12 EC Final Legal Challenge. The standard pathway has no required specialisation. A separate, selective Madrid dual degree has additional requirements.
components: Skills Development and Legal Challenge I: Introduction to Law and Legal Reasoning (SLC1001)
Skills Development and Legal Challenge II: Thinking Like a Lawyer (SLC1002)
Skills Development and Legal Challenge III: Legal Research (SLC2001)
Skills Development and Legal Challenge IV: Conflict Prevention and Resolution (SLC2004)

courses: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

core: Multi-level public law: Constitutional Law, International and European Law and Law of the European Union, which teach constitutional structures, the international legal order and the EU legal order and how international and EU law take effect in national legal systems
Comparative private law: Introduction to Private Law and Private Law, which teach family, contract, property and tort law (and private international law) from a comparative and European perspective

Foundations of law: Foundations of Law (legal history, legal philosophy and the economic analysis of law) and Philosophy of Private Law, which give the historical, philosophical and economic foundations of positive law

Legal skills track: Skills Development and Legal Challenge I to IV (Introduction to Law and Legal Reasoning, Thinking Like a Lawyer, Legal Research, Conflict Prevention and Resolution), which teach legal reasoning and argumentation, finding and evaluating legal sources, legal writing and research, and conflict prevention and resolution
Criminal law, criminal procedure and administrative law as compulsory second-year fields of national and comparative law
Independent legal research through Legal Research and the Final Legal Challenge, which includes an individual paper, public defence and final portfolio.
adjacent: Law and contemporary social problems through legal challenge projects and electives such as EU Law and Inequality, Criminal Sciences and Policy, and Privacy.
Conflict prevention, negotiation and dispute resolution through the skills sequence, with advocacy supported by practical legal exercises.
questions: How do European, international and national law interact to shape the current and future legal landscape?
How do legal systems compare, and how do lawmakers' choices differ across them?
How does law respond to contemporary social problems such as inequality, access to justice, crime, technology and human rights?

trace: surveys the legal systems of the world and the main fields of law (constitutional, administrative, criminal, international and human-rights law, and property, contract and tort law) and reads case law and performs trial simulations; it directly implements the general introduction to legal systems and fields of law on which the target's public-law, private-law and criminal-law courses rest

teaches human rights as positive law (rights treaties, monitoring mechanisms, case law) and then their historical and philosophical development; it directly implements the fundamental-rights protection taught in Constitutional Law and International and European Law and the philosophical side of Foundations of Law
Examines criminal liability and punishment through case analysis, advice memoranda and argument in a simulated legal-aid clinic.

teaches the sources, subjects and organisation of public international law, the use of force, international criminal, refugee and environmental law, and treaty compliance; it directly implements the international-law half of International and European Law

compares the constitutional and administrative law of five legal systems: government institutions, limits on government power, guarantees of rights and judicial review; it directly implements Constitutional Law and the comparative approach of the target, and covers administrative law only at introductory depth
Compares property, tort and contract law across several legal systems. Legal briefing, comparative research and simulated mediation develop legal analysis and negotiation.
Studies EU institutions, sources, remedies and free movement, and applies EU law to practical problems and national settings.
Examines EU institutions and policymaking through empirical work on European Parliament committee amendments.
Compares democratic and autocratic institutions and political participation, using comparative evidence and a research memo.
Connects international-relations theory with global institutions and conflict. A Security Council simulation develops negotiation and resolution drafting.

analyses the causes of violent and nonviolent conflict, conflict transformation and peacebuilding at regional, national and international levels, drawing on law among other disciplines; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the conflict theories and resolution mechanisms of Conflict Prevention and Resolution, without teaching negotiation, mediation or moot court
Uses consequentialism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics to develop moral reasoning. Reflective and research essays build normative argument.
Compares classical and contemporary European and non-European thought on rights, society and political authority.

gives a chronological overview of modern history (1815-2025), including popular sovereignty, national self-determination and the world wars; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the legal-history strand of Foundations of Law, which examines the political, social and cultural events that shaped European legal systems, without teaching legal history

teaches microeconomic principles (supply and demand, game theory, the theory of the firm, market structure) and macroeconomic fundamentals; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the economic-reasoning strand of Foundations of Law, without teaching the economic analysis of law

teaches the theory of rhetoric and argumentation from classical sources to contemporary public discourse; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the argumentation and persuasion skills of Thinking Like a Lawyer, without teaching legal argumentation
Practises public speaking, debate and storytelling through community-engaged teaching, complementing oral communication skills.
Studies persuasion, framing and ethics through applied communication projects and research.
Develops a historical research question and critical work with evidence, culminating in a substantial paper. The methods support independent inquiry outside legal doctrine.

trains students to recognise misinformation, assess the credibility of claims and sources and think critically; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the finding and evaluating of sources taught in Introduction to Law and Legal Reasoning, without teaching legal source-finding

covers logic and discrete mathematics, including formal logic and valid inference; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the deductive-inference and legal-syllogism training of Thinking Like a Lawyer, without addressing legal reasoning
Examines governance, justice and participation through sustainability cases and applied policy advice.

teaches qualitative research design, the interpretation of meaning and reflection on power dynamics in research; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the research-design and interpretive skills used in independent research projects, but not to doctrinal legal research
Applies sociological theory to institutions, stratification and inequality, supporting the study of social problems alongside law.
Applies social theory, including Black feminist, postcolonial and decolonial perspectives, to inequality and institutions.
Uses social movement theories and Environmental Justice Atlas cases to examine mobilisation, inequality and environmental justice.
Studies civil society, solidarity, social movements and public spheres through a research project on a civic organisation or initiative.

surveys the empires of world history and theories of their rise and fall, including their oppressive features; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the colonial roots of inequality and of international law, in historical rather than legal terms
Uses primary sources, interviews and research to study gendered lives, rights and activism in North America.

examines AI fairness and bias, privacy, responsibility and accountability from philosophical and psychological perspectives; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the target's AI-and-the-law legal challenge and privacy questions, without teaching AI or data-protection law

examines how film, photography and music address systemic racism, power and just futures in American history and life; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the study of racial inequality and its representation, not to legal doctrine

teaches research design, sampling, and descriptive and inferential statistics; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the empirical evidence used to study social problems and is the formal prerequisite of Public Economics
Uses public economics to analyse efficiency and equity, including taxation, welfare and redistribution.

alternatives.label: Comparative, European and International Law
alternatives.labelReason: Seven law courses provide the core. Political institutions, ethics, rhetoric and historical research support comparative analysis and argumentation.
alternatives.concept: Compare legal systems and study how constitutional, private, criminal, European and international law work. Use political science and philosophy to examine institutions and legal reasoning, and develop argumentation and research skills.
progression: Law, Society & Justice precedes dependent law courses. Introductory rhetoric precedes advanced persuasion and public speaking. Comparative Politics precedes European Union Politics.

alternatives.label: Law, Justice and Social Change
alternatives.labelReason: Law and human rights are studied alongside sociology, social movements, ethics, history and public economics.
alternatives.concept: Study how law responds to inequality, criminal justice and other social problems. Combine human rights and public law with sociology, social movements, ethics and the economics of redistribution.
alternatives.distinctness: The plans share 14 courses. This plan adds ten courses in sociology, historical inequality, AI ethics, media and race, and methods and public economics. The closest plan gives greater weight to private law, EU institutions, international relations and argumentation.
progression: Law, Society & Justice precedes dependent law courses. Introductory and modern sociology precede advanced social theory. Research Methods & Statistics precedes Public Economics.
traceOverrides: explores law from legal, social and normative perspectives, including the relationship between law and society and the concept of justice, and performs trial simulations; it directly implements the law-in-society and justice perspectives of the target's approach to contemporary social problems

teaches human rights as positive law and their historical and philosophical development; it directly implements the human-rights theme of the target's legal challenges (including the role of non-governmental organisations in international human-rights protection)

teaches criminal accountability, the justification of punishment and interdisciplinary research on organised crime; it directly implements the target's crime-and-punishment legal challenge and criminal-policy questions, but not criminal procedure

includes refugee law, environmental law, the right to self-determination and Third World Approaches to International Law; it directly implements the international-law themes of the target's legal challenges on environmental protection and human rights

compares how constitutions guarantee rights and restrict government power and how judicial review protects them; it directly implements the fundamental-rights protection that underlies the target's rights-based social-problem questions

teaches EU fundamental rights, citizenship and the free movement of persons; it directly implements the rights and citizenship content behind the archive electives EU Law and Inequality and EU Citizens' Rights and Remedies
Uses consequentialism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics to develop moral reasoning. Reflective and research essays build normative argument.
Compares classical and contemporary European and non-European thought on rights, society and political authority.
Compares democratic and autocratic institutions and political participation, using comparative evidence and a research memo.

analyses the causes of violence and conflict, structural inequality, identity-based grievances, reconciliation and radicalisation; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the social causes and remedies of conflict alongside the target's conflict-resolution and human-rights themes
Studies persuasion, framing and ethics through applied communication projects and research.
Examines governance, justice and participation through sustainability cases and applied policy advice.

teaches qualitative research design, interpretation of meaning and reflection on power dynamics; it makes a specific complementary contribution to the interpretive study of social problems and of the people affected by them

candidates.label: Law and contemporary social problems: human rights, criminal justice, inequality and social movements
Negotiation, mediation, dispute resolution and moot-court advocacy
candidates.reason: Principles of Private Law includes simulated mediation and negotiation. Criminal Law & Criminal Justice includes simulated legal advice and oral argument. Rhetoric, negotiation, business law and peace studies add complementary practice. The closest option already contains much of this core. The remaining coursework would shift towards business or political conflict and would lack sustained legal mediation, procedure and advocacy.

candidates.label: Spanish law and the Spanish and European law dual degree
candidates.reason: Annex 4a confirms a selective four-year Madrid dual degree. UCR does not provide Spanish law or the prescribed partner-university sequence.

selection.assessment: Two distinct options are defensible. The closest follows comparative, European and international law. The related option focuses on law and social change, with ten different courses in each direction. Negotiation and advocacy are supported within coursework but do not form a third coherent legal programme. The selective Madrid dual degree requires Spanish legal study and its own partner sequence.

blocks: Foundations of law and introduction to legal systems

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Foundations of Law teaches legal history, legal philosophy and law and economics as the foundations of positive law; UCR has no jurisprudence or legal-history course, and Ethics, Introduction to Political Philosophy, Modern History and Introduction to Economics contribute related perspectives without directly addressing the legal-historical, legal-philosophical or economic-analysis-of-law content of the component.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Philosophy of Private Law applies normative theories of justice to private-law doctrines; Ethics teaches the general normative theories but no UCR course addresses private-law doctrine from a philosophical standpoint, so the relationship is contextual.
Constitutional, administrative, EU and international law

Comparative Constitutional Law covers the institutions of government, limits on government power, guarantees of rights and judicial review across five legal systems, the subject of Constitutional Law; it is narrower on European and international constitutionalism and adds administrative law.

Introduction to Public International Law covers the sources, subjects and organisation of international law, the use of force and treaty compliance, the international-law half of International and European Law; the EU half is aligned separately with Law of the European Union.

Foundations of European Union Law covers the EU institutional framework, legal order, fundamental rights, citizenship and free movement, the subject of Law of the European Union at a more introductory level.
Comparative Constitutional Law introduces administrative decision-making, judicial review, remedies and procedural fairness. Maastricht develops administrative law in a dedicated second-year course.
Principles of Private Law covers property, tort and contract law comparatively across several legal systems, the subject of Introduction to Private Law (family law is not named in its description).
The UCR private-law course covers comparative property, tort and contract law. Maastricht develops private law over two compulsory courses.
Criminal law, criminal justice and human rights
Criminal Law & Criminal Justice covers criminal accountability, the legality principle, justifications and excuses and the justification of punishment, the subject of Criminal Law.

Explicitly unmatched after semantic review: Criminal Procedure covers investigative measures, pre-trial detention, prosecution and the criminal trial from a comparative perspective; Criminal Law & Criminal Justice is already the counterpart to Criminal Law and does not teach criminal procedure.
Peace & Conflict supplies conflict analysis and peacebuilding. UCR also practises mediation in private law, but has no equivalent dedicated legal conflict-resolution and advocacy sequence.
Legal skills, argumentation, communication and research

Both develop introductory legal reasoning and case analysis. UCR uses case briefs, interpretation, demand letters and mock trials. Maastricht teaches legal sources and drafting in a dedicated skills sequence.

The Art of Rhetorical Communication teaches the theory of rhetoric and argumentation, which corresponds to the legal-argumentation part of Thinking Like a Lawyer (structure and evaluation of arguments, persuasion); it does not teach legal syllogisms, the legal challenge or legal reasoning and covers only part of the component's scope.

Maastricht teaches legal research methodology and writing in a dedicated course. UCR develops case-law research in its law courses and offers separate historical, qualitative and empirical research training.
Maastricht requires an individual legal paper, public defence and final portfolio. UCR displays optional independent research alongside it.
Society, inequality, justice and social change
The 48 EC elective phase follows a learning plan and includes limits on non-law, introductory and internship credits. The exact selection is left open.

notes.text: UCR offers comparative private and constitutional law, criminal law, international law and EU law. Maastricht adds compulsory criminal procedure, more dedicated administrative law and a sequenced legal research and skills curriculum.

Maastricht requires 48 EC of restricted electives and a 12 EC Final Legal Challenge with an individual paper, public defence and portfolio. UCR offers optional independent research alongside its interdisciplinary coursework.

audience.comparisonExplanation: The closest UCR option studies comparative, European and international law. The second connects law with social change through human rights, criminal justice, sociology and public economics. Maastricht gives more time to compulsory legal doctrine, skills and research.

curriculum.limitation: This comparison follows the standard European Law School bachelor. The third-year electives follow an approved learning plan.

componentNotes.y3-01: Up to 24 EC may be non-law. Introductory electives are capped at 6 EC and a legal internship at 12 EC.
componentNotes.y3-02: Pass the Legal Research challenge before registering. The 12 EC component includes an individual paper, public defence and portfolio.
